title: The Same Difference, Twice Over
scopeNote: This keeps the parameterised two-group model and the live consequence of intercept non-invariance, reduced to a single control that holds the observed difference fixed while moving its source. The full configural, metric and scalar ladder, the separately movable loadings and intercepts, and the item characteristic lines for all four items stay in the longer version.
summary: Two groups differ by 0.20 on a four-item scale. One slider moves that difference between being entirely one item behaving differently and entirely a real difference in the trait, without the observed means changing at all.
learningObjectives: Explain why an observed mean difference is not yet a finding about people.
Distinguish an intercept difference from a difference in the latent mean.
Explain why the total score cannot distinguish the two.
Say what scalar invariance requires and what it licenses.
Explain why a significant difference in a large sample does not settle the question.
Recognise that concluding bias from a group difference is the same error in the other direction.
interactionTypes: a judgement about what a significant group difference establishes
a live control that holds the observed difference fixed while changing its source
item-level differences redrawn as bars that always sum to the same total
a live verdict on whether the means may be compared
a parameter table showing which item behaves differently
a guided setting in which the whole difference is real
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with the source of the difference on a native range input reporting its value in text. Every parameter is in a real table with row and column headers, and the table states in words which items behave the same way, so the figure is never the only route to the information. Bars carry their value as text and the bar representing an item behaving differently is labelled in words as well as coloured differently. The verdict tile states in words whether the means may be compared and carries a non-colour state signal. The chart description gives all four item differences, their total, and both scale means. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
dataStatus: Two fictional groups, called A and B, with no nationality, ethnicity, language, region or culture. Every figure is a parameter set by the control rather than an estimate from data, and nothing here is or could be a claim about any real group.
simulationNotes: The expected answer to an item is intercept + loading * latent mean, with group A as the reference at a latent mean of zero. Loadings are equal across groups throughout, so metric invariance always holds and only intercepts are ever at stake. The single control holds the observed scale-mean difference fixed at 0.20 and blends its source: the latent mean of group B rises in proportion to the blend, while the extra intercept on item 3 falls, arranged algebraically so that the observed difference is constant by construction. Each item's observed difference is its own intercept difference plus its loading times the latent difference, which puts the entire difference on item 3 at one end and spreads it across all four items in proportion to their loadings at the other. The four bars therefore always sum to the same total while their shape changes completely, and that shape is what an invariance test inspects. The bar axis is fixed at the largest value any blend can produce, so the figure does not rescale as the slider moves and make every setting look alike. Simplifications: parameters are set rather than estimated and carry no sampling error, where a real test compares nested models and returns a degree of confidence; only one item's intercept can differ, so partial invariance across several items is not represented; and loadings never differ, so metric invariance is never tested.
readmeTopic: why a group difference in scores is not yet a group difference in the trait
